_about: The story's words. The indictment is read one count per death, in order; after the last count, a death adds one of the addenda. {years}, {total} and {year} are filled in by the core. death_titles head the indictment by the zone you died in. interludes are read between a zone's boss and the next zone, by the zone just left. The verdict follows the last built zone's boss (the Executor, in this build); its last line is mechanical and says what the build holds.
case: IN THE TRIBUNAL OF THE LAST HOUR, WHICH SITS AFTER EVERYTHING ELSE HAS RISEN · Case 2081-1 · The City of Meridian, and its nine million mornings, against the Defendant
sentencing: There is a court that sits after the last hour has been struck. It keeps no calendar, because it has no further use for one. It tried you there. You do not remember the trial. The clerk says nobody does, and that this is a mercy the court extends to everyone, whether they want it or not.
The verdict was guilty. The sentence was Corrective Return: you would be carried back to the night of the fourteenth of March, 2081, and you would stand in the doorway, and you would stop yourself.
The Bailiff of Hours has carried prisoners down the years since before the years were counted. It is patient the way stone is patient. It has never once mistaken a date.

Fifty years early, in a city that does not yet know what it is waiting for. The night you were sent to lies at the far end of half a century, and there is only one road there, the one everybody walks: an hour, and then the next hour. Begin.
counts: COUNT THE FIRST. That on the evening of the fourteenth of March, 2081, the Defendant let themself into the Meridian Observatory with a key that had been given to someone else, a long time before, for a different reason.

COUNT THE SECOND. That the Defendant there woke the instrument called the Long Door. They had built it themself, over eleven years, and registered it with the city as a clock for measuring weather. In a sense it was.

COUNT THE THIRD. That the Long Door was made to hold a single evening open, the way a hand holds a door, so that one person inside that evening would never have to leave it; and that the Defendant knew what a door held open lets out.

COUNT THE FOURTH. That at fourteen minutes past nine the Defendant stopped the clocks of Meridian, and with them the morning of nine million people, and called it, in their notebook, a small adjustment.

COUNT THE FIFTH. That the people of Meridian are still in that evening. They are not dead. Dead would be a kind of ending, and this court knows endings well. They are waiting for a tomorrow that does not come.
COUNT THE SIXTH. That the one person the Long Door was built to keep is among them, in a kitchen with the light on, halfway through a sentence, and does not know.
COUNT THE SEVENTH. That the Defendant, alone outside the stopped city, walked its streets for thirty-one days and was seen by no one, because there was no one left who could look up.
COUNT THE EIGHTH. That the Defendant came to this court of their own accord, declined counsel, and offered one sentence in their defence, which the clerk took down exactly: I would do it again.

COUNT THE NINTH. That the court finds that sentence to be the crime. A deed is over once it is done. A person who would do it again is a deed that has not happened yet, and must be met before it does.
COUNT THE TENTH. That the person you are walking toward, at the far end of the fifty years, is you: older by every year this court has added, waiting, and certain.
addenda: ADDENDUM. The Bailiff reports that the Defendant fell in {year} and was returned without complaint. The years are added. The court notes that it did not ask whether they were wanted.
ADDENDUM. The clerk asks that the record show the Defendant gets a little further each time. The court agrees to show it. The years are added anyway.
ADDENDUM. No new charge. The court wished only to remind the Defendant that it is still sitting, and that it has nowhere else to be.
ADDENDUM. A juror asked how many times a person may be sent back before they become someone else. The question was struck from the record. The years were not.
time_served: The court adds {years}. Your sentence now runs to {total}.
victory: You stand over yourself in the circle, and your older face looks up at you without fear. They say: I would do it again. Then the sky above the summit tears like wet paper.

It comes through all at once: a mass larger than the mountain, bubbling, blind and covered in eyes, piping to itself in a voice like a choir of flutes. The stones melt. The summit runs like wax. You are drawn up toward a mouth the size of the night.

Now you understand what the court never did. The Long Door was a ritual, not a clock. You built it to hold one evening open for one person, and it opened onto the outside instead, and the thing outside heard it, and came. You led it here. Your older self stopped time because a stopped moment was the only lock strong enough to hold it at the threshold.

The Tribunal knew only that time had stopped and that something had to be fixed. No one in your own timeline could get near the Defendant, so they reached into another timeline for a version of you more amenable to their cause. You. Nobody knew what stopping your older self would let in, except your older self, who learned to stop time to keep this reality from being eaten.
Your sin was never the stopping of time. It was the door.

The heart of the Idiot God is sealed in this build. You can now stop time yourself: press T, for 3 seconds, and up to 6 with the Stopped Clocks in the Holding. The Clemency from this run has been added to your record.

bailiff.name: THE BAILIFF OF HOURS
bailiff.title: It has carried the condemned down the years since before the years were counted. It is not cruel. It is punctual.

witness.name: THE WITNESS
witness.title: Every court needs one who saw. This one has watched the ice since before there was ice, and it has already seen what you will do.

defendant.name: THE DEFENDANT
defendant.title: You, older by every year the court added. You would do it again. You are about to.

executor.name: THE EXECUTOR
executor.title: It carries out its orders to the letter. It has never once asked who signed them.

chief.name: THE SECTION CHIEF
chief.title: He has a list of names. Yours is on it, and so is everyone you hired.

pioneer.name: THE PIONEER
pioneer.title: The expedition's walking frame. The ice took its pilot, and taught it to walk on its own.

escort.name: THE ESCORT
escort.title: The Executor's little sister. It goes ahead to see that the doors are open.

waiting_city.title: THE YEARS BETWEEN
lines: The Bailiff of Hours goes down on one knee in its own court, and the stopped clock above the bench says nothing, which is what it has always said. It was not sent to bring you back. It was sent to make sure you never arrived.
It does not get up. The court, which does not lose things, loses track of you for a while, and the clerk writes that down too.

You have what nobody else in 2031 has: the next fifty years, read once, out of order. You know which harbours will flood and which will hold, which small firms will matter, which bridges will never be built. You do not need luck. You have the minutes.

By 2044 the company has your name on its door and two floors of a tower in the new city. People call it foresight. A newspaper calls you the most patient investor in Meridian, and you read the article twice, because you already know how the paper ends.

Count the first says the key was given to someone else, a long time before, for a different reason. It was given to Ines Calder, the Observatory's first keeper. In 2039 she took it north on the Long Patience, to measure the weather at the top of the world, and the ice kept her, and the key, until someone went to fetch it. You know who. You have seen that face in mirrors.

So in the spring of 2046 you pay for a ship of your own and sail north to fetch it first. Behind you the city is busy and bright and has thirty-five years left. Ahead is the White Waste, where the year turns so slowly that the court keeps someone there to watch it.

white_waste.title: WHAT THE WITNESS SAW
lines: The Witness lowers its arms. The ice it grew into goes clear, the way a window does when the frost on it gives up, and inside it is a woman in an old red coat, asleep, with a key on a string round her neck. You take the key. She does not wake.

Then the Witness speaks, which the court's records say it has never done. It has watched you, it says, the whole way down the years, and it has seen what you will do with the key. You will do a thing so terrible that time itself will stop rather than go on past it.

You ask what the thing is. The Witness opens its mouth and nothing comes. It is not refusing. Whatever it saw has no words yet, and the Witness falls silent in the middle of a breath, as if the sentence it was about to say had been taken from it.

You sail home with the key in a lead box. By then the company is worth more than some countries, and in 2047 you buy the old house on Calder Hill above Meridian and fill its wings with laboratories. For ten years you spend the money on one question: how a person keeps time from breaking.

Physicists, clockmakers, two theologians, a woman who mends church bells. They work through the nights and find nothing that holds, and the money goes, and you sign for more. Somewhere in the house you are always listening for a clock to stop.

In the autumn of 2056 it is not a clock. Men in grey coats come up the lawn in the rain, all of them with the same face, and the first of your scientists dies at the conservatory door before anyone hears a shot. It is your house. You know every room of it. Go.

glass_house.title: THE ORDERS
lines: The Executor settles onto its treads in the wreck of the conservatory, and its eyes close, one wheel at a time, until the house is dark and quiet and full of rain.

In the turret, behind the last of its cannons, is a steel case, and in the case are its orders. They are typed on the house's own typewriter, the one in the safe room with the sticking e. They are dated the fourteenth of March, 2081. They are signed in your hand.

Raid the house on Calder Hill. End the work. Kill whoever you must, the scientists first. And under the signature, in ink, in the handwriting you have used your whole life: Time must break. If it does not, everything else will, which will be much worse.
You read it twice. You were sent back to stop yourself. At the far end of twenty-five years, you are already stopping you.

You have thought about letting yourself die. More than once, on the long nights in the house, it seemed the cleanest way: no Defendant, no door, no evening that never ends. But the court does not allow it. Every time you fall, the Bailiff collects you and sets you on your feet again, and the years are added, and you go on.

So it seems that this version of you must kill that version of you. Fifty years have come down to one evening. On the fourteenth of March, 2081, you climb Mount Meridian toward the Observatory on its summit, where the Long Door stands in a circle of old stones, and the evening light does not move, because it is always twenty-one fourteen. Someone you trained is waiting on every terrace. They all wear your coat.
